utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Registrar, would you have the accused brought in, please? (The accused was brought in). Mr. Aleksovki, would you please be seated. Please put your headset on and, anyway, first I would like to know everybody hears me. Does the Prosecution hear me? Fine. Does the Defence hear? Mr. Aleksovki do you hear in your own language? Are things being interpreted into your language? Fine. Then before we begin the hearing, I would like to have the appearances for the Prosecution and the Defence. Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. My name is Niemann and I appear with Mr. colleges Mr. Meddegoda and Mr. Marchesiello. I am assisted at the bar table by Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: And the appearances for the Defence please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, my name is Mikulicic. I am defence counsel for the accused Zlatko Aleksovki.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. This morning, during the hearing, we have to review three, but actually four motions. There is a motion from the Prosecutor on the collecting of certain depositions, another motion from the Prosecutor on the protection of witnesses, of certain witnesses that is, and two defence motions, one dealing with defects in the form of the indictment and the other a request for a separation of proceedings. I think the best thing would be to take them chronologically, if you have no problem with that. I see that they were prosecution motions having to do with depositions that were filed on 5th June. Then there was the motion of the Prosecutor for the protection of witnesses and victims on 13th June and the Defence filed on 19th June, two motions which were put together in one motion, one dealing with the defects in the form of the indictment, and the other the separation of proceedings. If the parties agree, I suggest that we just begin by -- begin with the oldest one, oldest one, chronologically, 5th June, dealing with certain depositions from the Prosecution, specifically those relating to the Blaskic case. You did not ask for in camera here, Mr. Niemann; is that correct? You did not request in camera for that part of the motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honours. It occurred to us that the proceedings could proceed in public unless, of course, it got into a discussion of the particular witnesses involved. In that event we might ask that the sound that goes outside of the courtroom be turned off if that becomes necessary, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That is fine. Excuse me, Mr. Niemann, I forgot to tell you that you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Your Honours, I am not aware of whether or not there is to be a great deal of opposition to this motion from the Defence. In the event that there is not opposition from it then we rely on our written submissions that we have already tendered in the motion itself. Perhaps just dealing very briefly with the matter, the Prosecution brings this motion essentially on two bases, one in order to relieve the difficulty associated with bringing witnesses twice to The Hague, and what we say is inconvenience and trauma associated to witnesses on having to testify on two occasions, if it can be resolved by the parties to take their evidence by way of deposition. We submit, your Honours, that deposition evidence in these circumstances would overcome that necessity. Secondly, your Honours, we see it as a means by which we can proceed with taking evidence in preparation for trial, and hence as a means of expediting the proceedings and hopefully ensuring that the trial itself, should there be no contest, or significant contest, in relation to the evidence which needs to be resolved before The Chamber, would considerably facilitate a much more expeditious proceeding than that which would take place if we simply waited until the trial proper. It is on those bases that in our submission it is appropriate that an order be granted that deposition evidence be obtained from the witnesses. There is considerable discussion, I think, necessary on the actual procedure which would take place before the Registrar. It is a matter upon which I would wish to expand, depending on the approach that your Honours take to the matter. But, having regard to the fact that we have set, in some detail, the bases of our motion, in our -- the basis of our argument in the motion, might I invite my friend from the Defence to express his position on it? And then perhaps I can expand in reply on the matters that he would wish to raise at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, I know that you have read the Prosecutor's motion. You heard the explanations that had to be brief because the Prosecutor is prepared to discuss the issue with you. First we have to know whether in principle you agree, and then of course to see whether in a private session we might come to an agreement. I read your writings, and I believe that I understood that you did not object to the principle, but that you did express several observations. And I must say that I did not really understand everything that you meant, specifically in addendum 2. I think this is the proper time for you to explain what you meant, first in regard to the principle what you think about this in terms of accelerating the proceedings. You know this Tribunal, and specifically this Trial Chamber is very interested in having speedy trials, and therefore would like to know what your opinion is, Mr. Mikulicic, both on the principle and the methods to be used. First speak about the principle. And I give you the floor now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. On the part of the Defence, I can say, in the first place, that we, too, are eager to expedite the proceedings, as you have just indicated. Therefore, any motion, any measure that may be taken by this court which is in the interest of expediting the proceedings and is not to the detriment of the interests of my client will always meet with our support and understanding. Speaking in principle, as we had indicated at the last status conference, the Defence, in principle, is not opposed to certain witnesses who will be coming to The Hague to testify in the Blaskic case, and who might also appear in this case, should make a deposition within the framework of certain rules. Therefore, in principle, the Defence is agreeable to the proposal of the Prosecutor in that sense. In our submission, -- in their submission of 5th June, 1997 my learned colleague, the Prosecutor, on page 7 of his motion, under B to F has specified certain circumstances and conditions within which such a deposition would be taken from witnesses. If I may be allowed, I should like to comment briefly on those conditions. Regarding point B, the Defence agrees. Regarding point C, the Defence would prefer that this 7 days notice could be extended to make it longer. Therefore, the Defence would prefer if it could be given notice of the Prosecutor's intention to take a deposition from a specified witness 14 days ahead of that deposition. Regarding point D, the Defence is also agreeable. Regarding point E, we also have no opposition to it, as well as regarding point F, we have no objections. So much about the motion of the Prosecution. Have I made myself clear now? If necessary I am at your disposal for additional clarifications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, thank you. Therefore, we will say that you agree on principle and as well as the methods concerning the six points mentioned by the Prosecutor. Mr. Niemann, would you like to take the floor again?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, briefly your Honour, certainly we have no problem with 14 days notice, if that is of more assistance to the Defence. I think we should have no difficulty in complying with that. So, it can be that just noted as part of your Honours orders should your Honours decide in favour of the motion. Alternatively we could amend our motion if that makes it more convenient to the court to read 14 rather than 7 days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think that we are moving forward. The principle is that both parties agree. This does not require a decision. The Registrar will simply put it in the transcript, and we will set these methods to be used in an order that we will give. In the transcript, we will state that there were agreements on points A, B, modified C, with the 14 days advance notice, D, E and F, that there is total agreement. Yet, I would like to go to the very end of things. If I have understood you properly so Mr. Mikulicic and everybody understands one another, in your response dated 18th June, apparently you made comments about two witnesses. If I have understood you correctly, this is no longer relevant, and there were 7 or 8 witnesses that were mentioned by the Prosecutor. I am not going to mention their names, since they are under seal, but for the Prosecutor there are 8 witnesses. Let me repeat the two questions. One the question for the Prosecutor, there are 8 witnesses not 7. I want to know if we agree on that. I would like to go back, so we finish with this issue, I would like to go back to your answer. I did not quite understand. Apparently you had certain reservations about two witnesses, I think that is what it was. I will not of course give their names, so I cannot specify them any more than that. Perhaps we could assign a number to them, perhaps that might be witness number 1 and witness number 5. But I am not quite sure I understood what your reservation is. Perhaps you have waived something and it is no longer valid. Mr. Mikulicic, could you explain yourself further on this issue, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. My reservation has to do with the two witnesses that you have mentioned, insofar as the documents disclosed by the Prosecutor did not include the statements of those witnesses. However, this has been remedied, and the Prosecutor has provided us with these two statements, so that that objection no longer stands. If I may make just one further additional point. In the Prosecutor's motion that we are talking about, dated 5th June, 1997, and please I should like to apologise in advance if I was not careful enough in studying it, I did not identify the position of the Prosecutor regarding the presence of the accused during the taking of the depositions. It is the position of the Defence that the accused should also be present in addition to the Prosecution and the Defence when these depositions are being taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, certainly the Prosecution would wish that the accused be present, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right then, in the minutes or in the transcript we will say we can confirm the methods to be used. But we confirm that the accused be present. Before we complete our discussion of this motion there was another point, there was the measures asked of the Tribunal, that of this witness you do not want the name revealed either to the public or the media. I suppose that the Defence agrees with that point?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, with respect to these witnesses listed individually, the Defence has no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine. Let me turn to each of my colleagues to see whether they have any comments or observations they wish to make, or remind me of something I may have forgotten. Fine. The motion is settled. This will not give rise to a decision. Everybody agrees we want to expedite the proceedings. We will not render a decision specific to this subject. However, when the Prosecution is ready, perhaps Mr. Niemann could -- we are not going to render a decision specifically related to this. This will be noted in the minutes of the Registry, but when you are ready, Mr. Niemann, you will inform the Registry who will ask, and here I think I can say this under Rule 54, will render an order which will define the more specific methods to be used for the deposition. Do we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine. Then if there are no other comments, as I said, we can move to the second motion, following the same chronology. This is also from the Prosecutor on the motion to protect victims and witnesses. This was a motion dated 13th June, which was answered by Mr. Mikulicic on 10th July. Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Again, your Honour, this motion deals with the issue of disclosure beyond that which is necessary for the Defence to prepare their case, and is designed, in our submission, to ensure that witnesses' names are not in the public domain, or published in newspapers, and of that sort of publication, which we say is not in the interests of justice for that to occur. So it is expressly directed to that end. It is not in any way suggested to deal with the ability of the Defence to proceed to obtain evidence in reply to the Prosecution case. Your Honours, I think, as we understand it, the main area of concern that the Defence had with our motion in this regard related to the question of the specification of the witnesses themselves, in terms of names and/or other descriptions applicable to them. That has been remedied. Our original motion was of a general nature and related to all witnesses. The Defence position on that was they should at least know who it is that we are referring to. That, your Honours, has been resolved. We have now provided the Defence, Mr. Mikulicic, with a list of all the witnesses to whom we are referring and to what this particular motion applies. I have provided that list to Mr. Mikulicic this morning. It is a letter addressed to him, but if The Chamber would be assisted by seeing this list and our covering letter, and if Mr. Mikulicic has no objection to it I am happy to hand that to The Chamber for your assistance. I see Mr. Mikulicic has no objection to it, so perhaps I might hand to your Honours a copy of the letter that we gave to him this morning, which sets out the names of the witnesses and the dates that the statements were to -- the date that the statements were disclosed to him. It is in respect of those particular witnesses mentioned there, on the attached list, to whom we are referring. Your Honours, I should just state at this stage that it is possible that further witnesses may come to light. We are not expecting very many, but it is possible that further witnesses may come to light. In that event we will raise the matter with Mr. Mikulicic, and if agreement cannot be obtained, then we will file a separate motion in relation to those specified witnesses. Your Honours, I do not think, at this stage, I am aware of any other objection to the Prosecution motion. As I say, it is not a motion for anonymity, it is a motion designed to protect the names of the witnesses being put into the public domain. As I understand Mr. Mikulicic's position he has no objection to that. I think that the specification of the names may have resolved any objection he had. I might leave my submission at this stage until we hear further from Mr. Mikulicic on the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Niemann, just one moment, please. Perhaps it is a translation problem. On page 3 in the French version of your motion in paragraph 6, this may also be in the English version it says that the Prosecutor respectfully requests The Chamber to grant the following request. There is a first but there is no second, you see. I think that the -- is this one which sort of was put into -- came out of the computer somewhat miraculously. Or was there a second request?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: There is no second request. I apologise your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That is all right. Let me turn to Mr. Mikulicic. If I understood you correctly, your comments that were expressed on 10th July specifically related to identifying elements which were not given to you. In principle you were in agreement. I would like to ask you, Mr. Mikulicic, whether you confirm what has just been said, ever since you have received this identifying information?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was our main concern. The Defence was, in principle, opposed to the Prosecutor's motion for protection measures, regarding witnesses and for their names not to be disclosed to the public without indicating which witnesses they supplied to. And the Defence understood the Prosecutor's request as being in the bonam partem and felt such bonam partem motion is not in accord with the rules of procedure of this Tribunal. That is why the Defence insisted of the need -- on the need for learning of identification information regarding the witnesses concerned. I can confirm that this morning I received from Mr. Niemann a list of the witnesses concerned, to whom this proposal applies. The Defence has no objection to these witnesses from the list being covered by the measures proposed by the Prosecution, that is that their names are not released in the public domain at this stage of the proceedings. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will take note of this agreement. We are not going to draft a decision. Everybody agrees, but it will be indicated in the Registry's minutes. But the Tribunal will render an order on the protective measures, which will be taken at the request of the Prosecutor. If my colleagues have no questions, Judge Riad, Judge Shahabuddeen, if they do not we can move on to the third fourth motions which are put together by the Defence as part of the writings dated 18th June, dealing with the defects, and the form of the indictment, and a request for separation of proceedings. Mr. Mikulicic, by the way I want to go backward just a little bit. I have a terminology question, because our Tribunal is using a lot of Latin and you talked about bonam partem agenda. It is a bit rusty. What is bonam partem. What do you mean by that? What does it mean bonam partem?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I use this Latin term in order to describe good procedural rules, only for that purpose. I do not know if that is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. All right, we can now back to your own motion, Mr. Mikulicic. I give you the floor. There is the separation of proceedings and the question of the defects in the form of the indictment which you have alleged as to that indictment, 19th June, and the response of the Prosecutor. All right, I give you the floor, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Allow me to start from the second motion, that is the motion for a separation of trial, because I believe that no further argument will be required after this, since my learned colleague, Mr. Niemann, in his submission, has agreed with the proposal of the Defence for a separate trial. Therefore, I think that we are in agreement as far as that is concerned, and I therefore propose that if necessary Mr. Niemann could make his comment and then we can go on to the defect in the form of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic is quite right. We raise no objection to a separate trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Therefore, the Registry's notes will note that, that there will be separate trials. Mr. Mikulicic, as regards the fourth request, dealing with the defects in the form of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Regarding this motion, I should like to remind your Honours of the motion of the Defence of the 19th June, when the Defence sought, as concisely as possible, to indicate certain defects in the indictment as it sees them. I still stand by the objections presented in my motion in writing as regards the actual form of the indictment, but as a brief reminder let me just say a few words. The main objections of the Defence regarding the form of the indictment have to do, actually, with several points. The first remark or the first objection in the view of the Defence is that in the text of the indictment, and I am referring to paragraph 31, on page 8 of the indictment, of the 13th November, 1995, no indication is given of the place, time, persons and manner of the execution of the alleged crimes, which should be the object of this trial. And further to that, it is the submission of the Defence that no detailed description has been given of any criminal conduct of the accused, my client, Mr. Aleksovki. In view of such a form of the indictment, the Defence feels that the accused is unable to prepare his defence because he is not fully aware of the facts of the indictment. A further objection of the Defence has to do, in the submission of the Defence, with the imprecision in the definition of the key notions, that is the notion of the actual facility Kaonik, and the notion of the function that the accused performed in that facility. In the supporting materials to the indictment, this Kaonik facility is described in various ways. Once it is referred to as a camp, then as a prison, then again as a detention camp, and there is no need to list any further descriptions. The same applies --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Where are you referring to, what paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I am talking about chapter 31.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Similarly, in the supporting materials, and that is not reflected in the indictment itself, the status of the accused is also defined in different ways. In this connection, we come to the third section of our objections, and that is the question of the mental state of the accused in relation to the alleged crimes. In the submission of the Defence, it is our view that the indictment has not indicated the subjective position of the accused or rather the form of his culpability. Does the indictment refer to direct negligence, or possible, dolus directus or dolus eventualis? Does it indicate negligentia, or culpa, or mental state? I do not wish to tire you with the details, because it is all contained in my motion, and the Defence proposes to this Trial Chamber that in view of the objections expressed with respect to the indictment, which the Defence considers to be defects in form, the proposal to the Trial Chamber is that in accordance with the submission of the Defence it issues orders to the Prosecution to amend the indictment accordingly. That would be my submission, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: This is a question I would like to ask, Mr. Mikulicic. What do you mean by the subjective relationship? Are you talking about the mens rea.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When talking about the subjective attitude of the accused towards the crime, I am referring to the form of his guilt. And we find that the indictment has not specified that, as I have just explained. I do not know whether I have made myself clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We now must ask the Prosecutor, since it has heard the requests of the Defence asking for a modification of the indictments, specifically as regards the definition of the form of guilt, what the Defence refers to as the subjective relationship, in relation to the alleged crimes, and more important specifications as to time and place. Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Your Honours, I will make a few observations concerning Mr. Mikulicic's submissions, and then I might ask my colleague, Mr. Meddegoda, if he wishes to add further to that, your Honours. Your Honours, firstly, I would like to deal with what the indictment itself does say. I think that is illustrative, and assists in determining this question. Firstly, in paragraph 7, the indictment tells us who it is that is charged and gives a description of the person. That is a description not only in relation to family, but to where he comes from, and gives a brief recital of his previous positions held by him and, in our submission, puts the accused, Mr. Aleksovki, into the context of the indictment, and then goes on and says that in 29th January 1993 he left his previous position and became commander of a prison facility at Kaonik near Busovaca. Your Honours, in our submission, that is very precise in its statement as to what the position held is. It is very precise as to the location of the place where it is that the Prosecution alleges the accused committed the crimes with which he is charged. It then goes on to deal with where he was after that particular period, from January 29th 1993, until May 1993. It describes him as becoming the head of the district HVO in the Heliodrome Prison in Mostar. Your Honours, we have there, in our submission, a number of things. We have a precise description of who the accused is in terms of his name and his previous employment and positions. We have a precise description of where he was at times relevant for the indictment. Now, your Honours, in paragraph 20 and 21, this is expanded and added to. Again, we have Mr. Aleksovki referred to in paragraph 20, as initially being an official in a prison at Zenica, and then him going to Kaonik. So there is a repetition of that. It expressly states him as being in charge of the Kaonik prison. It then goes on to deal with the question, in our submission, his position there and his responsibility there. In our submission, that responsibility being relevant to the charges against which -- which are alleged against him. It says that he was in charge of the Kaonik prison. He was in a position of superiority to every one else in the camp. As commander he met with the international committee of the Red Cross, which, in our submission, puts -- is some material, or some detail, some particular, of his position of command. That he met with other international organisations while in that position, namely the European community monitoring mission, again being particulars of his authority and responsibility. That authority and responsibility, in our submission, is relevant to the charges -- to the offences with which he has been charged. We deal with the question of knowledge, which Mr. Mikulicic has discussed, that the indictment, he alleges, is deficient in. But there it provides that these people gave him lists of detained persons, and acknowledged his position as commander of the facility and his understanding of the Geneva Conventions in relation to the detention and treatment of prisoners. To some extent we get an insight, perhaps more than one would ordinarily encounter in an indictment. It goes further than most indictments one would ordinarily see in national jurisdictions in addressing his mental state, his state of mind, his responsibilities. In paragraph 21, it then goes on and specifically and expressly states that the accused Zlatko Aleksovki has demonstrated or exercised his control over the detention facility of Kaonik prison in a variety of ways, including, but not limited, to formal meetings and so forth of the nature I have discussed. Then it goes on to allege allowing the unlawful interrogation of detained persons and allowing them to be used as human shields. In our submission, that is indeed -- it provides a considerable number of particulars in relation to the type of crimes which are alleged, and at the time and place when those crimes are said to have occurred. One then goes, in our submission, your Honours, to paragraph 31, which provides even greater specificacy and detail in terms of time, in terms of what it is that is alleged against him. That paragraph says that from January 1993, at least until the end of May 1993, which, in our submission, is very specific in terms of time, having regard, of course, to the position that he occupied and the nature of the crime with which he has been charged, that is very specific, because it is dealing with his role as commander of this prison, for a specified time. It says that Mr. Aleksovki accepted hundreds of detained Bosnian Muslim civilians from the HVO or their agents into his custody at the detention facility in Kaonik. The detainees were from a widespread area but not exclusive to Vitez and Busovaca municipalities. Many of the detainees under his control were subjected to inhumane treatment, including, but not limited to excessive and cruel interrogation, physical and psychological harm, forced labour (digging trenches) in hazardous circumstances, being used as human shields and some were murdered or otherwise killed. We have here, in our submission, a very detailed specification of the matters with which the Prosecution alleges that the accused -- offences it alleges the accused committed. Then finally we have the charges themselves. This specifies with whom it is said that he has committed these crimes. It again specifies the period of time, this being more specific, because it specifically says 1st January to 31st May. It then relates back and incorporates in the charge those paragraphs, at least some of those paragraphs to which I have referred. It specifies that he did it individually, some aspects of the crime were committed individually, some aspects of the crime were committed in concert. He ordered -- he instigated, ordered and otherwise aided and abetted in the planning, preparation, execution of unlawful treatment, et cetera in the Lasva Valley. The Lasva Valley is specified. The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina is specified. Then in the alternative it is alleged he knew or had reason to know that subordinates were about to do the same, had done so and failed to take necessary and reasonable measures to prevent such acts or punish the perpetrators thereof. In our submission, the indictment is very clear in what it alleges. It is very clear at the time and place where it is alleged to have occurred. And it also deals, to some extent, with the giving particulars of the -- what the Prosecution alleges the accused knew about these events and what he failed to do about them. Your Honours, the indictment, in our submission, is not intended to be the whole prosecution case. It never has been intended for that purpose. Indeed, Rule 47B provides that the indictment shall set forth the name. It does that, the particulars of the suspect, it does that, and a concise statement of the facts of the case. It does that, and the crime with which the suspect is charged. It does that. It does everything that the statute and the rules in our submission requires to be done by the indictment. Indeed, we would say it goes further and is much greater in its specification and detail than that which is required by the rules or by the statute of the Tribunal. In addition to that, your Honour, in terms of fair trial, in terms of notice to the Defence, there is not only the indictment with which the accused can acquaint himself with the allegations of the Prosecution. There is extensive discovery provided for under the rules, which discovery has been as diligently complied with by the Prosecutor as has been possible in the circumstances. That extensive discovery, in our submission, puts the accused on full notice of the Prosecution case, full notice of the Prosecution case, a very substantial period of time prior to the hearing. Indeed, the Defence, in our submission, would in no way be inhibited from preparing their case having regard to a lack of detail, considering the extent of discovery that has been made and will continuously be made right up to the period of the time of the trial. In our submission, the Defence have nothing that they can point to to suggest that they have been inhibited so far by the nature of the discovery with which they have been provided. In addition to that, your Honours, there is, of course, the opening address, which generally speaking is extensive and covers in detail the allegations again which the Prosecution make, and then, in that time, sets out such matters as the elements of the offence and the evidence which the Prosecution will specifically be seeking to rely on in order to prove its case. All of these matters are noticed. All of these matters are designed to assist the accused in being aware of the charges against him, to assist him in the preparation of his defence and, in our submission, are more than adequate. That is all I wish to say on the matter at the moment. Perhaps my colleague may wish to add to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Meddegoda?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: That is correct, my Lord.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Meddegoda, would you take the floor, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: If I may expand, your Honours, on the submissions that have been made by my learned friend Mr. Niemann. The Prosecution has, in its response to the form of the -- to the motion on the defects on the form of the indictment, has set out very extensively the rules of law governing the statuted provisions governing the indictment that is submitted by the office of the Prosecutor. As your Honours will see, there is Rule 47B of the rules of procedure and evidence read with Article 18(4) of the statute. It is the submission of the Prosecutor that there has been full compliance with the provisions set out therein. The Prosecutor has, in preparing the indictment, set out in detail the name and particulars of the suspect. The Prosecutor has also set out a concise statement of the facts of the case and of the crime with which the accused is charged. To the indictment is also attached the statement of fact setting out the conduct, the evidence against the accused, and the conduct of the accused in relation to the crimes with which he has been charged in the present indictment. It is also the complaint of learned defence counsel, your Honours, that the Kaonik facility has not been properly defined in the indictment. I think my learned friend, Mr. Niemann, has sufficiently dealt with that issue, and I do not think I should go into further detail on that matter. Another submission of the counsel for the accused is that the indictment is vague. Your Honours, it is the Prosecution's submission that each count of the indictment has to give the accused a warning of the nature of the crimes with which he is charged, and also has to set out the factual basis of those charges. The Prosecutor, your Honours, has articulated each charge specifically and separately, and identified the particular acts in order to sufficiently inform the accused of the charges against which he has to defend himself. As the Trial Chamber has held in the Tadic indictment position the purpose of the indictment is very succinctly to demonstrate that the accused allegedly committed the crime. It is the submission of the Prosecutor, your Honours, that the Prosecutor has very succinctly or more than succinctly demonstrated that the accused has committed a crime and therefore it is the submission of the Prosecutor that the indictment is not vague. It is also alleged, your Honours, that the indictment fails to set forth the factual allegations and regarding the identities of the victims. Your Honour, it is the respectful submission of the Prosecutor that the indictment, together with the supporting material disclosed to the Defence, provides sufficient factual details regarding the identities of the victims in this case. The supporting material, your Honours, contains numerous names of victims, and also sufficient details regarding the identities of those victims. Therefore, your Honours, it is the Prosecutor's submission that in that material -- with that material has been supplied sufficient details identifying the victims, numerous names of victims have been given with the supporting material, and the victims have been clearly identified in that material. So therefore, your Honours, it is the Prosecution submission that the Defence motion on the defects of the form of the indictment has no merit, your Honours, and that the Prosecutor has complied with the provisions of the statute and the rules of procedure and evidence. The Prosecutor has given the accused sufficient notice of the nature of the crimes with which he is charged. The Prosecution has given the accused the factual basis for those charges. The Prosecution has, in its indictment, and the supporting material and the statement of fact, concisely described the underlying conduct and participation of the accused which forms the basis of its culpability, and therefore the Prosecutor has provided the accused with sufficient detail to allow him to prepare his defence adequately. Therefore, your Honours, it is the respectful submission of the Prosecutor that the motion, that the Defence motion on the form of the indictment be denied. Is there any other matter your Honours would wish me to address you on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the Defence wish to exercise its right to reply? Does the Defence wish to reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Then do so, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Fully acknowledging the learned explanations of my learned colleagues, on the Prosecution side, the Defence continues to believe that the indictment is incomplete and imprecise. The Defence wishes, once again, to draw attention to the actual wording regarding the statement of facts in connection with the crimes alleged to have been committed by client, Zlatko Aleksovki. Allow me to point to two places. In paragraph 31 of the indictment the Prosecution states that many of the detainees under his control, the reference is to the control of the accused -- how can one explain the word "many"? The Defence would be content with the form of the indictment if it had indicated the names of the people who were subjected to inhumane treatment. The expression "many" is vague. The same can be said of the worst form of culpability, and that is that some were killed or otherwise deprived of life. The Defence wishes to underline, once again, that the Prosecution should indicate, by name, who were the persons who were murdered or otherwise killed, and under which circumstances, so that this might be linked to the possible culpability of the accused. That would be our main objection, regarding the imprecision of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. Judge Shahabuddeen wishes to make a comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, in paragraph 10 of your written motion you plead that the indictment fails to specify and to define the status of the object Kaonik. The Defence does not know whether it was a prison, a detention camp, a prisoners of war camp, a cantonment or something else. Now I leave out the word "cantonment" for the moment, because I have not succeeded in tracing it. Maybe it exists in the indictment, but I have not, as yet, chanced upon it. But I believe the other expressions occur, do they not, in the indictment, prison is referred to, detention is referred to. Take, for example, paragraph 7 of the indictment, refers to Kaonik as a prison facility. Paragraph 31, paragraph 20, refers to it as a detention facility, prison and a camp. So that the indictment does so describe Kaonik. What I am trying to get at is; what exactly is the objection? Is it the objection that the indictment describes Kaonik in several ways? And is it your contention that it should describe Kaonik in one way only?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. That was precisely the intention of the Defence, to require that the Kaonik facility be described with precision, because depending on that precise definition of the site where the alleged crimes covered by this indictment were committed, the actual definition of the status of the accused depends, and thereby also the form of his culpability, if any, of course. That is what the Defence has tried to indicate. I am sorry if we were not clear enough, and not precise enough, and I apologise to your Honours if that was the case. But this was our intention. Thank you. I hope I have managed to answer your question, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. I think I understand. Now, may I pose a question to Mr. Prosecutor? It relates primarily to a paragraph of the indictment, paragraph 36, which I think you read out, Mr. Niemann. If I may say so, without disrespect, it is a bit of a mouthful. We have there that he is being charged for having done certain things, both individually and in concert, a point which you made. Then it goes on, in the fourth line from the bottom of the paragraph, to say: "... and, or in the alternative he knew or had reason to know, that subordinates were about to do the same, or had done so, and failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent such acts or to punish the perpetrators thereof." Now, I have followed you in your reading of Rule 47B and your submission that the ingredients therein specified have been supplied by the indictment. But would it be the case that the mere supplying of the specifying ingredients would not, by itself, satisfy the imperatives of the statute if, in their totality, they fail to accord to the Defence fair trial I think that is stated in the master provisions or somewhere or other in the statute. I need not recite the text to you. Would it then follow that mere compliance with the service requirements of Rule 47B, would not suffice if it leaves the Defence in a position of uncertainty as to what exactly it is required to respond to? We have, in Rule 49, a joinder provision stating that two or more crimes may be joined in one indictment. But you have followed the usual scheme, which visualises that one offence will be charged in one count. There is some jurisprudence, I believe, of the Tribunal on the question, and I would like you very much to address me briefly on the implications of that jurisprudence for paragraph 36. A distinction exists, I know, between charging more than one offence in one count, and charging one offence as having been committed by different methods. But I seem to need your assistance in appreciating exactly what is it that is being said in this paragraph? Is the accused being required to defend himself on different offences, or is he being required to defend himself on one offence, which is alleged to have been committed by different methods?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the paragraph I read out was paragraph 37, but it provides the detail. Your Honours, what is sought in paragraph 37, as opposed to the counts themselves, that is counts 8, 9 and 10, what is done there is the theory of liability has been set out; and true it is that the theory of liability, as is provided for in Article 7(1) of the statute, and Article 7(3) of the statute is provided for. Paragraph (3) of the Article 7 being the alternative, that is knew or had reason to know. Article 7(1), setting out the theory of liability that he committed it individually, in concert with others, planned, instigated, and otherwise aided and abetted. Your Honour, the theory of liability does vary, having regard to the nature of the particular offences charged here. What we have here, your Honour, is three counts. Dealing with conduct in relation to a camp over a period of time, the nature of the charge is that it is alleged that there was inhumane treatment, for example, in Count 8. But that inhumane treatment may have varied according to particular prisoners and particular instances that occurred during that period of time. If I can perhaps assist by an illustration. Say, for example, there had been a charge of persecution, or say there had been a charge of genocide, or a crime against humanity, could that have been included there? Those crimes would not specify, for example, that genocide was committed by this individual, would not necessarily specify that genocide was committed by the individual, because he killed X, victim X. Genocide would be alleged, because it was a crime committed against a particular group of people, with the specified intention. So there would not be specificity in terms of that. Likewise here, with the nature of these charges, because you are dealing with a mixture of people who are being contained in the camp, people have different status’s. So people who come into the camp could be, in fact, people who are combatants, no longer combatants but are prisoners of war and kept in that facility. The Prosecution's allegations do not limit itself to that. The Prosecution's allegations are all embracing. They cover the people who may fall into that category, or arguably could fall into that category. As your Honours know a different provision of the Geneva Conventions would apply to people who are prisoners of war as opposed to civilians who were captured in the net and brought into this camp. You have two different categories of people. We say that is all alleged in the indictment itself, because we say it is an attack on the Muslim population. We say that is all embracing, so it can cover both types of categories. The indictment reflects that in dealing with theory of liability. There also is, because you are dealing with the period of time, him being commander of the camp over a specified period, there are a number of acts which are committed, some which we would say he is directly involved, and some which we would say he merely aided and abetted, or participated in planning or preparation. And there is a variety of these instances. The indictment, again, attempts to cater for all of them, to put him on notice of all of these allegations which are being made. If I may expand on that. For example, it may be said that a person was beaten in the camp. The accused -- it is not suggested on the evidence that the accused was aware at the time that that person was beaten. Evidence may be brought however that he subsequently became aware of that, he subsequently became aware of the fact that a guard, in his camp, committed a series of beatings. The evidence of the Prosecution in that instance may be that nothing ever happened, there is no evidence whatever of him ever taking action against that person. That, in our submission, would be one theory of liability, we would say catered for in the indictment and would come out in the course of evidence, come out in the opening address and be dealt with and become obvious on the supporting material. We say the statute and the rules do not require the Prosecutor to go in and specify every particular instance. If you are dealing with massive crimes such as genocide or a massive crime against humanity it would be impossible the indictment would be thousands of pages long because you would be attempting to deal with each one. Further, your Honours, you might have a situation where it may be alleged that prisoners that were kept in the camp were sent out during the course of a day to dig trenches, and the trenches were being dug on the front line. These people were being exposed to fire from the enemy and being put in a dangerous situation. They may be prisoners of war, they may be ex-soldiers or, indeed, they may be just civilians who were brought in and kept in the camp for no other reason than the fact they were Muslim. It may be a differentiation there, because there is a different method of dealing with people according to their categories in that regard. In our submission, your Honours, this accused may not be liable for requiring these people to dig trenches because he stayed back in his prison camp and commanded that and looked after it. The Prosecution are not alleging that. The Prosecution would allege he aided and abetted in that because he knew what was happening to these people and he permitted these people to be taken out of his camp, people under his control, he aided and abetted in the commission of that crime. Again, we have a different theory of liability. Again, we are dealing with the substantial nature of the crime. So, in our submission, that is why the theory of liability specifies, in our submission, the full gambit of crimes which the Prosecution alleges this accused has committed in terms of his responsibility, his criminal responsibility. So that is the reason why it is recited in this way. It is entirely possible that the evidence may not come up to proof on one aspect of it. If that happens then of course that falls. But the Prosecution's allegations, at this stage, are that the Prosecution case will come up to proof on each one of these allegations, in an individual sense, according to specific components of the evidence. And if on its face it appears perhaps less specific than what one encounters when you are dealing with an individual count of murder or an individual assault and battery or something, that is because, in our submission, the nature of these offences are that one needs to deal with the magnitude of them, and the magnitude of them, as such, that there are limits, of course, as to just how specific we can be. Otherwise you would end up with, you know, 2,000 counts or something like that, because you would be dealing with each particular act. In our submission that is not an economic way or indeed a fair and reasonable way to deal with the allegations, and is not within the nature of the crimes themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand you, and I owe you the explanation of saying yes, I was intending to read paragraph 36, but I realised that you had been reading from paragraph 37. I would appreciate the position to be this: that the words which I read though carrying in a chapter in Counts 4 to 7 really belong to what may be described as a chapeau to a further itemisation of distinct counts each of which relates to a specific offence. Perhaps that is the answer to the question which I raised. So the specific counts occurring beneath the generalised chapeau would remove any appearance of obscurity or difficulty which might be presented by the general words of the opening or introductory section. I understand you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to make two comments of a general nature, and then end these proceedings. I would like to thank Judge Shahabuddeen very much, who saw the difficulty which is not semantic in this indictment. Perhaps I might say to the Defence, first of all, I suppose that they did it, that many things were written, and the Tribunal has ruled many times, but not in one case was there a preliminary motion referring to the indictment, to the defects of the form of the indictment. In that respect there is case law which is being formed. That is my first comment there is the Delic case through the Tadic case through the Blaskic case, also which is covered by the same indictment. We have tried to reconcile the relevant provisions of the statute. That is 1898 statute of 45 and 47 of the rules. There are two times here. There is the time of the indictment, which necessarily must be briefer. Then what happens right after the initial appearance when the Defence has more important rights. The second comment I would like to make is the one that Judge Shahabuddeen did, not to say again because it was done very relevantly, but it is the word in the alternative. I have a more general comment. The indictment, perhaps, suffers from the time that has gone by since it was drafted, in light of the different requests which are more specific, that the judges have heard. It is true that on several occasions the judges have expressed themselves, since 1995, in these general terms. We have often called the Prosecutor's attention -- Mr. Niemann knows this -- to, for example, not here, words like "around", "about", "approximately"; and "alternatively" is sort of in between the specification of facts and the specification of law, which Mr. Niemann has just spoken to, referring to the count under Article 7(1) and 7(3). These are general comments which do not prejudice the Trial Chambers. Generally speaking Judge Riad has no comments he would like to make, asks no questions. Perhaps I would like to turn to the Defence. You know, Mr. Mikulicic, the 60 day time period for the preliminary motions since the initial appearance should be -- should expire on 29th June. Can we ask you today whether you have any other preliminary motions you tend to file? At any rate the time period has expired but in other changes the Trial Chamber, for factual reasons, has granted extensions of these time periods. I think that we asked this question during the status conference of 6th June. We therefore consider that the 60 day period has expired. There is no other motion from you, which you would, at that point, have to justify; is that correct? There are no others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence counsel has no further motions pending. We have exhausted our motions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, and Mr. Mikulicic, I want us to understand. I am not talking about any other motions. You have all the rights you want to exercise in order to file motions. I am speaking about Rule 72 and 73 of the rules dealing with preliminary motions. Ordinarily, as in 73B, it says, in the 60 days following the initial appearance. This period expired on 29th June. Nonetheless, if justified at the request -- of the request they can be extended. I believe that you have completed all the preliminary motions that you wanted to make. This is something you can confirm now because we can then go forward towards setting up a schedule for the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I mean. I have no preliminary motions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will now respond with a decision. In fact, it will be the only decision emanating from this morning's proceedings both having to do with case law and -- case law referring to the defects in the form of the indictment. Now, we can turn to the Prosecutor so that we can try to set a date for the trial, although you do know, Mr. Mikulicic, that there are physical problems which we are experiencing for the time being in this Tribunal since at this point we have only one courtroom. But you know this, and also you are aware of the fact that a second courtroom should be built soon. If there are no other comments Mr. Prosecutor. Do you have any other comments you wish to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, have you any other comments you would like to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no comments or objections; but may I just make a brief statement, without wishing to sound pathetic, I do appeal to you when ruling on the object of today's debate that you bear in mind, though I am sure you will do that anyway, that today and in this place the history of a new jurisprudence is being made and that any decision taken is of the utmost significance, not only for this case, but for all future cases which will be tried by this Tribunal. Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. The court stands adjourned.
